newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Portugal, Indonesia end Timor talks; agree to more.
newsitem.headline: Portugal, Indonesia end Timor talks; agree to more.

text.p: Ambassadorial-level talks between Indonesia and Portugal on the question of East Timor ended on Thursday with an agreement to meet again in a few weeks; however, no date was set for the next session.

"The delegations of the two governments will return to their capitals and have agreed to resume the talks at a later date," said Jamseed Marker, the special representative for U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan, who chaired the talks.
Marker gave few details except to say that the negotiations, which began on Monday, were constructive. "I am an incurable optimist," he said.
He told reporters the new talks would be held "within weeks" and again in New York, adding: "It should be fairly soon. We do want to keep these things going."

Indonesia occupied East Timor in 1975 after a civil war erupted following Portugal's withdrawal from its colony. In 1976 Indonesia incorporated the territory as its 27th province, but this has never been recognised by the United Nations.
One source close to the talks said that no breakthough had been anticipated at this stage but that "interesting" issues not discussed previously were aired at the session.
Indonesia was represented by its U.N. ambassador, Nugroho Wisnumurti, while Portugal sent Fernando Neves, its special envoy for East Timor.

Marker, a former Pakistani U.N. ambassador, said he would be travelling to South Africa shortly to brief President Nelson Mandela, who has offered to help the United Nations with the long-running dispute.
"I am waiting for the dates depending on President Mandela's schedule," he said.

Several diplomats said that Mandela's involvement was a positive development as no government leader of his stature previously had shown such interest in the Timor controversy. Mandela, they said, would be able to speak with authority to heads of state and government as well as the Timorese.

After two days of talks at the United Nations in June, the foreign ministers of Portugal and Indonesia agreed that senior officials of the two sides would embark on intensive negotiations on East Timor this summer.
U.N.-mediated talks between the foreign ministers of Indonesia and Portugal have been continuing since 1983 with a goal of finding an internationally acceptable solution to the problem.
